claim: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using Hallmark and KEGG gene sets from MSigDB revealed 17 gene sets that were significantly upregulated (FDR q < 0.25) across both S2-013 and CFPAC-1 cell lines following 2-week BQ exposure.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using Hallmark and KEGG gene sets from MSigDB (Liberzon et al., 2011; Subramanian et al., 2005) revealed 17 gene sets that were significantly upregulated (FDR q < 0.25) across both cell lines following 2-week BQ exposure (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data from S2-013 and CFPAC-1 cells treated with BQ, followed by GSEA analysis using established gene set databases.

claim: Twelve of the 17 significantly upregulated gene sets are ontologically related to antigen presentation and contain MHC class I, MHC class II, and/or APP genes such as TAP1 in the leading edge.
source: Twelve of these gene sets (highlighted in purple) are ontologically related to antigen presentation and contain MHC class I, MHC class II, and/or APP genes such as TAP1 in the leading edge.
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA results showing enrichment of antigen presentation-related gene sets in BQ-treated cells.

claim: Certain gene sets, such as allograft rejection (KEGG), graft versus host disease (KEGG), and antigen processing and presentation (KEGG), are composed almost entirely of APP genes.
source: Certain gene sets, such as allograft rejection (KEGG), graft versus host disease (KEGG), and antigen processing and presentation (KEGG), are composed almost entirely of APP genes (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA plots shown in Figure 1C demonstrating enrichment of these specific gene sets.

claim: APP genes were robustly upregulated in a dose- and duration-dependent manner in CFPAC-1 cells.
source: Heatmap analysis showed that APP genes were robustly upregulated in a dose- and duration-dependent manner in CFPAC-1 (Figure 1D) and S2-013 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by heatmap visualization of RNA sequencing data showing increased APP gene expression with increasing BQ dose and treatment duration.

claim: The effect size of APP gene upregulation was generally smaller for S2-013 cells compared to CFPAC-1 cells.
source: The effect size was generally smaller for S2-013 cells, likely because they are resistant to DHODH inhibition due to efficient nucleoside salvage, as we previously reported (Mullen et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of RNA sequencing data between the two cell lines and is explained by previously published findings on nucleoside salvage in S2-013 cells.

claim: S2-013 cells are resistant to DHODH inhibition due to efficient nucleoside salvage.
source: The effect size was generally smaller for S2-013 cells, likely because they are resistant to DHODH inhibition due to efficient nucleoside salvage, as we previously reported (Mullen et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previously published work by the authors.

claim: Publicly available RNA-seq data from human A375 melanoma cells treated with the clinically approved DHODH inhibitor teriflunomide showed that teriflunomide caused a rapid (within 12 hr) and duration-dependent increase in MHC-I/II and APP transcript levels.
source: Publicly available RNA-seq data from human A375 melanoma cells treated with the clinically approved DHODH inhibitor teriflunomide (Tan et al., 2016) corroborated our findings, as teriflunomide caused a rapid (within 12 hr) and duration-dependent increase in MHC-I/II and APP transcript levels (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of publicly available RNA-seq data from a published study.

claim: MHC-I heavy chain transcripts (HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C) are consistently upregulated in response to BQ across diverse cancer types.
source: This confirmed that MHC-I heavy chain transcripts (HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C) are consistently upregulated in response to BQ across diverse cancer types (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from a panel of human cancer cell lines treated with BQ.

claim: 2-week BQ treatment of B16F10 murine melanoma cells caused dramatic APP gene upregulation.
source: To optimize conditions for in vivo studies, we tested the long-term response and observed that 2-week BQ treatment of B16F10 murine melanoma cells also caused dramatic APP gene upregulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from B16F10 cells treated with BQ for 2 weeks.

claim: Flow cytometry confirmed a marked increase in cell surface MHC-I levels in nonpermeabilized live CFPAC-1 cells following a 2-week BQ treatment.
source: Flow cytometry confirmed a marked increase in cell surface MHC-I levels in nonpermeabilized live CFPAC-1 (Figure 1G) and B16F10 (Figure 1H) cells following a 2-week BQ treatment, confirming that transcriptional upregulation of APP genes results in greater cell surface antigen presentation.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data measuring cell surface MHC-I expression.

claim: Flow cytometry confirmed a marked increase in cell surface MHC-I levels in nonpermeabilized live B16F10 cells following a 2-week BQ treatment.
source: Flow cytometry confirmed a marked increase in cell surface MHC-I levels in nonpermeabilized live CFPAC-1 (Figure 1G) and B16F10 (Figure 1H) cells following a 2-week BQ treatment, confirming that transcriptional upregulation of APP genes results in greater cell surface antigen presentation.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data measuring cell surface MHC-I expression.

claim: Transcriptional upregulation of APP genes results in greater cell surface antigen presentation.
source: Flow cytometry confirmed a marked increase in cell surface MHC-I levels in nonpermeabilized live CFPAC-1 (Figure 1G) and B16F10 (Figure 1H) cells following a 2-week BQ treatment, confirming that transcriptional upregulation of APP genes results in greater cell surface antigen presentation.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation between RT-qPCR data showing increased APP gene transcription and flow cytometry data showing increased cell surface MHC-I.

claim: BQ treatment caused a rapid (8 hr treatment) and dose-dependent accumulation of dihydroorotate and N-carbamoyl-aspartate (upstream of DHODH) in CFPAC-1 cells.
source: The results demonstrated a rapid (8 hr treatment) and dose-dependent accumulation of dihydroorotate and N-carbamoyl-aspartate (upstream of DHODH) as well as depletion of pyrimidine nucleotides UTP and CTP (Figure 1I and J) and other pyrimidine species (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS metabolomics data from CFPAC-1 cells treated with BQ.

claim: BQ treatment caused a rapid (8 hr treatment) and dose-dependent accumulation of dihydroorotate and N-carbamoyl-aspartate (upstream of DHODH) in B16F10 cells.
source: The results demonstrated a rapid (8 hr treatment) and dose-dependent accumulation of dihydroorotate and N-carbamoyl-aspartate (upstream of DHODH) as well as depletion of pyrimidine nucleotides UTP and CTP (Figure 1I and J) and other pyrimidine species (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS metabolomics data from B16F10 cells treated with BQ.

claim: BQ treatment caused depletion of pyrimidine nucleotides UTP and CTP in CFPAC-1 and B16F10 cells.
source: The results demonstrated a rapid (8 hr treatment) and dose-dependent accumulation of dihydroorotate and N-carbamoyl-aspartate (upstream of DHODH) as well as depletion of pyrimidine nucleotides UTP and CTP (Figure 1I and J) and other pyrimidine species (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS metabolomics data from cells treated with BQ.

claim: On-target DHODH inhibition and resultant pyrimidine nucleotide depletion correlates with the transcriptional induction of APP genes and enhanced antigen presentation via MHC-I.
source: These results confirm that on-target DHODH inhibition and resultant pyrimidine nucleotide depletion correlates with the transcriptional induction of APP genes and enhanced antigen presentation via MHC-I.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation between metabolomics data showing pyrimidine depletion, RNA-seq/RT-qPCR data showing APP gene upregulation, and flow cytometry data showing increased cell surface MHC-I.

claim: Media supplementation with uridine rescued cell viability following BQ treatment in B16F10 cells.
source: As we previously observed (Mullen et al., 2023), media supplementation with uridine rescued cell viability (Figure 2A) and pyrimidine levels (Figure 2B) following BQ treatment and partially rescued viability following teriflunomide treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data from B16F10 cells treated with BQ with or without uridine supplementation.

claim: Media supplementation with uridine rescued pyrimidine levels following BQ treatment in B16F10 cells.
source: As we previously observed (Mullen et al., 2023), media supplementation with uridine rescued cell viability (Figure 2A) and pyrimidine levels (Figure 2B) following BQ treatment and partially rescued viability following teriflunomide treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data from B16F10 cells treated with BQ with or without uridine supplementation.

claim: Media supplementation with uridine partially rescued viability following teriflunomide treatment in B16F10 cells.
source: As we previously observed (Mullen et al., 2023), media supplementation with uridine rescued cell viability (Figure 2A) and pyrimidine levels (Figure 2B) following BQ treatment and partially rescued viability following teriflunomide treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data from B16F10 cells treated with teriflunomide with or without uridine supplementation.

claim: Uridine supplementation blocked mRNA induction of mouse MHC-I transcripts (H2-Db, H2-Kb, and B2m) by BQ in B16F10 cells.
source: Uridine supplementation likewise blocked mRNA induction of mouse MHC-I transcripts (H2-Db, H2-Kb, and B2m), as well as Nlrc5 (a major MHC-I transcriptional coactivator) and Tap1 (required for peptide import into the ER, a key step in MHC-I antigen presentation) by BQ (Figure 2C) or teriflunomide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), while uridine alone had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from B16F10 cells treated with BQ with or without uridine supplementation.

claim: Uridine supplementation blocked mRNA induction of Nlrc5 by BQ in B16F10 cells.
source: Uridine supplementation likewise blocked mRNA induction of mouse MHC-I transcripts (H2-Db, H2-Kb, and B2m), as well as Nlrc5 (a major MHC-I transcriptional coactivator) and Tap1 (required for peptide import into the ER, a key step in MHC-I antigen presentation) by BQ (Figure 2C) or teriflunomide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), while uridine alone had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from B16F10 cells treated with BQ with or without uridine supplementation.

claim: Nlrc5 is a major MHC-I transcriptional coactivator.
source: Uridine supplementation likewise blocked mRNA induction of mouse MHC-I transcripts (H2-Db, H2-Kb, and B2m), as well as Nlrc5 (a major MHC-I transcriptional coactivator) and Tap1 (required for peptide import into the ER, a key step in MHC-I antigen presentation) by BQ (Figure 2C) or teriflunomide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), while uridine alone had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the function of Nlrc5.

claim: Uridine supplementation blocked mRNA induction of Tap1 by BQ in B16F10 cells.
source: Uridine supplementation likewise blocked mRNA induction of mouse MHC-I transcripts (H2-Db, H2-Kb, and B2m), as well as Nlrc5 (a major MHC-I transcriptional coactivator) and Tap1 (required for peptide import into the ER, a key step in MHC-I antigen presentation) by BQ (Figure 2C) or teriflunomide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), while uridine alone had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from B16F10 cells treated with BQ with or without uridine supplementation.

claim: Tap1 is required for peptide import into the ER, a key step in MHC-I antigen presentation.
source: Uridine supplementation likewise blocked mRNA induction of mouse MHC-I transcripts (H2-Db, H2-Kb, and B2m), as well as Nlrc5 (a major MHC-I transcriptional coactivator) and Tap1 (required for peptide import into the ER, a key step in MHC-I antigen presentation) by BQ (Figure 2C) or teriflunomide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), while uridine alone had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the function of Tap1 in the antigen presentation pathway.

claim: Uridine supplementation blocked mRNA induction of APP genes by teriflunomide in B16F10 cells.
source: Uridine supplementation likewise blocked mRNA induction of mouse MHC-I transcripts (H2-Db, H2-Kb, and B2m), as well as Nlrc5 (a major MHC-I transcriptional coactivator) and Tap1 (required for peptide import into the ER, a key step in MHC-I antigen presentation) by BQ (Figure 2C) or teriflunomide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), while uridine alone had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from B16F10 cells treated with teriflunomide with or without uridine supplementation.

claim: Uridine alone had no effect on APP gene expression in B16F10 cells.
source: Uridine supplementation likewise blocked mRNA induction of mouse MHC-I transcripts (H2-Db, H2-Kb, and B2m), as well as Nlrc5 (a major MHC-I transcriptional coactivator) and Tap1 (required for peptide import into the ER, a key step in MHC-I antigen presentation) by BQ (Figure 2C) or teriflunomide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), while uridine alone had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from B16F10 cells treated with uridine alone.

claim: The same phenotype of uridine blocking DHODH inhibitor-mediated APP induction was observed in HCT116 human colorectal cancer cells.
source: This same phenotype was observed in HCT116 human colorectal cancer cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HCT116 cells treated with BQ with or without uridine supplementation.

claim: Cell surface MHC-I upregulation by BQ (24 hr treatment) was abrogated by uridine supplementation in B16F10 cells.
source: Concordantly, cell surface MHC-I upregulation by BQ or teriflunomide (24 hr treatment) was abrogated by uridine supplementation (Figure 2D), while uridine alone again had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from B16F10 cells treated with BQ with or without uridine supplementation.

claim: Cell surface MHC-I upregulation by teriflunomide (24 hr treatment) was abrogated by uridine supplementation in B16F10 cells.
source: Concordantly, cell surface MHC-I upregulation by BQ or teriflunomide (24 hr treatment) was abrogated by uridine supplementation (Figure 2D), while uridine alone again had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from B16F10 cells treated with teriflunomide with or without uridine supplementation.

claim: Uridine alone had no effect on cell surface MHC-I expression in B16F10 cells.
source: Concordantly, cell surface MHC-I upregulation by BQ or teriflunomide (24 hr treatment) was abrogated by uridine supplementation (Figure 2D), while uridine alone again had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from B16F10 cells treated with uridine alone.

claim: DHODH inhibitor-mediated APP induction is caused by pyrimidine nucleotide depletion.
source: These results demonstrate that DHODH inhibitor-mediated APP induction is caused by pyrimidine nucleotide depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that uridine supplementation, which restores pyrimidine levels, blocks APP induction by DHODH inhibitors.

claim: S2-013 cells with DHODH deletion (sgDHODH) require exogenous uridine for viability.
source: We have previously demonstrated that these cells require exogenous uridine for viability and experience profound pyrimidine depletion (>95% depletion of UTP and CTP) after 8 hr incubation in nucleoside-free media (Mullen et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previously published work by the authors.

claim: S2-013 cells with DHODH deletion (sgDHODH) experience profound pyrimidine depletion (>95% depletion of UTP and CTP) after 8 hr incubation in nucleoside-free media.
source: We have previously demonstrated that these cells require exogenous uridine for viability and experience profound pyrimidine depletion (>95% depletion of UTP and CTP) after 8 hr incubation in nucleoside-free media (Mullen et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previously published work by the authors.

claim: After 72 hr exposure to nucleoside-free media, sgDHODH S2-013 cells upregulated HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C.
source: After 72 hr exposure to nucleoside-free media, sgDHODH cells upregulated HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C, and this was reversed by adding back uridine (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from sgDHODH S2-013 cells cultured in nucleoside-free media.

claim: Upregulation of HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C in sgDHODH S2-013 cells exposed to nucleoside-free media was reversed by adding back uridine.
source: After 72 hr exposure to nucleoside-free media, sgDHODH cells upregulated HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C, and this was reversed by adding back uridine (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from sgDHODH S2-013 cells cultured in nucleoside-free media with or without uridine supplementation.

claim: Treatment with BQ did not further increase MHC-I mRNA expression in sgDHODH S2-013 cells exposed to nucleoside-free media.
source: Importantly, treatment with BQ did not further increase MHC-I mRNA expression (Figure 2E, compare blue and red bars).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from sgDHODH S2-013 cells cultured in nucleoside-free media with or without BQ treatment.

claim: BQ-mediated APP induction is an on-target phenomenon with respect to DHODH inhibition.
source: Together with our other data, these results indicate that BQ-mediated APP induction is an on-target phenomenon with respect to DHODH inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including uridine rescue experiments and genetic deletion of DHODH.

claim: Uridine addback rescued BQ-mediated loss of viability in B16F10 cells.
source: Since uridine addback rescued BQ- and teriflunomide-mediated loss of viability (Figure 2A, S2A), we queried whether BQ-mediated APP induction was caused by pyrimidine depletion per se, or if it was the result of some nonspecific downstream consequence of pyrimidine starvation, such as DNA damage or loss of cell viability.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data from B16F10 cells treated with BQ with or without uridine supplementation.

claim: Uridine addback rescued teriflunomide-mediated loss of viability in B16F10 cells.
source: Since uridine addback rescued BQ- and teriflunomide-mediated loss of viability (Figure 2A, S2A), we queried whether BQ-mediated APP induction was caused by pyrimidine depletion per se, or if it was the result of some nonspecific downstream consequence of pyrimidine starvation, such as DNA damage or loss of cell viability.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data from B16F10 cells treated with teriflunomide with or without uridine supplementation.

claim: Besides interferon gamma, BQ, teriflunomide, and GSK983, the only agent that induced APP gene transcription in the screen of CFPAC-1 cells was mycophenolate.
source: Besides interferon gamma (a positive control), BQ, teriflunomide, and GSK983 (another DHODH inhibitor), the only agent that induced APP gene transcription in this assay was mycophenolate, a clinically approved inhibitor of the de novo GTP synthesis enzymes inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 (IMPDH1/2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from CFPAC-1 cells treated with a panel of chemotherapy agents and small molecule inhibitors.

claim: Mycophenolate is a clinically approved inhibitor of the de novo GTP synthesis enzymes inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 (IMPDH1/2).
source: Besides interferon gamma (a positive control), BQ, teriflunomide, and GSK983 (another DHODH inhibitor), the only agent that induced APP gene transcription in this assay was mycophenolate, a clinically approved inhibitor of the de novo GTP synthesis enzymes inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 (IMPDH1/2).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about mycophenolate's mechanism of action.

claim: The effect of mycophenolate on APP gene expression was validated in B16F10 cells.
source: The effect of mycophenolate on APP gene expression was subsequently validated in B16F10 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), demonstrating that either purine or pyrimidine nucleotide depletion can induce cancer cell APP mRNA expression in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from B16F10 cells treated with mycophenolate.

claim: Either purine or pyrimidine nucleotide depletion can induce cancer cell APP mRNA expression in vitro.
source: The effect of mycophenolate on APP gene expression was subsequently validated in B16F10 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), demonstrating that either purine or pyrimidine nucleotide depletion can induce cancer cell APP mRNA expression in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that both DHODH inhibitors (which deplete pyrimidines) and mycophenolate (which depletes purines) induce APP gene expression.

claim: BQ-mediated APP induction in CFPAC-1 cells is not a general phenomenon that occurs downstream of DNA damage or some other response to therapy-induced stress.
source: While we cannot rule out the possibility that these agents induce APP transcription in other cell lines or under other dose/duration conditions, the inertness of these compounds (with respect to APP gene expression) in our screen suggests that BQ-mediated APP induction in CFPAC-1 cells is not a general phenomenon that occurs downstream of DNA damage or some other response to therapy-induced stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observation that multiple DNA-damaging agents and other stress-inducing compounds did not induce APP gene expression in the screen.

claim: HEK-293T cells display rapid (within 4 hr) transcriptional induction of MHC-I upon BQ treatment.
source: To elucidate the molecular pathway leading to APP induction downstream of pyrimidine depletion, we extended our findings to HEK-293T cells, which also display rapid (within 4 hr) transcriptional induction of MHC-I upon BQ treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HEK-293T cells treated with BQ for various durations.

claim: Neither ruxolitinib (a JAK1/2 inhibitor with activity against STAT3) nor GSK8612 (a TBK1 inhibitor), nor TPCA-1 (an IKK2 inhibitor) abrogated BQ-mediated APP induction in HEK-293T cells.
source: Neither ruxolitinib (a JAK1/2 inhibitor with activity against STAT3) nor GSK8612 (a TBK1 inhibitor) (Thomson et al., 2019), nor TPCA-1 (an IKK2 inhibitor) (Podolin et al., 2005) abrogated BQ-mediated APP induction (Figure 3A), despite blocking APP induction downstream of poly(dA:dT) and interferon gamma (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) as expected.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HEK-293T cells treated with BQ in combination with various pathway inhibitors.

claim: Ruxolitinib, GSK8612, and TPCA-1 blocked APP induction downstream of poly(dA:dT) and interferon gamma in B16F10 cells as expected.
source: Neither ruxolitinib (a JAK1/2 inhibitor with activity against STAT3) nor GSK8612 (a TBK1 inhibitor) (Thomson et al., 2019), nor TPCA-1 (an IKK2 inhibitor) (Podolin et al., 2005) abrogated BQ-mediated APP induction (Figure 3A), despite blocking APP induction downstream of poly(dA:dT) and interferon gamma (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) as expected.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from B16F10 cells treated with poly(dA:dT) or interferon gamma in combination with pathway inhibitors.

claim: Canonical regulators of MHC/APP expression (IFN-JAK-STAT, NF-κB, and cGAS-STING-TBK1) are dispensable for APP induction downstream of DHODH inhibition.
source: This indicates that these canonical regulators of MHC/APP expression are dispensable for APP induction downstream of DHODH inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that inhibitors of these pathways do not block BQ-mediated APP induction.

claim: The IKK2 inhibitor BMS-345541 mostly abrogated BQ-mediated APP induction in HEK-293T cells.
source: Interestingly, the IKK2 inhibitor BMS-345541 (Burke et al., 2003) mostly abrogated BQ-mediated APP induction (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HEK-293T cells treated with BQ in combination with BMS-345541.

claim: BMS-345541 effectively blocked BQ- and Ter-mediated APP induction at concentrations of 10 µM and 40 µM, but not 2.5 µM in HEK-293T cells.
source: BMS-345541 effectively blocked BQ- and Ter-mediated APP induction at concentrations of 10 µM and 40 µM, but not 2.5 µM (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HEK-293T cells treated with BQ or teriflunomide in combination with various concentrations of BMS-345541.

claim: The effect of BMS-345541 on blocking BQ-mediated APP induction was confirmed in B16F10, CFPAC-1, and HCT116 cells.
source: The effect of BMS-345541 was confirmed in B16F10 (Figure 3C), CFPAC-1 (Figure 3D), and HCT116 (Figure 3E) cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from multiple cancer cell lines treated with BQ in combination with BMS-345541.

claim: BQ treatment (24 hr) of HCT116 cells caused increased cell surface expression of MHC-I.
source: Furthermore, BQ treatment (24 hr) of HCT116 cells caused increased cell surface expression of MHC-I, which could be reversed by either uridine supplementation or by treatment with BMS-345541; neither uridine nor BMS-345541 alone affected cell surface MHC-I expression (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from HCT116 cells treated with BQ.

claim: BQ-mediated increase in cell surface MHC-I expression in HCT116 cells could be reversed by either uridine supplementation or by treatment with BMS-345541.
source: Furthermore, BQ treatment (24 hr) of HCT116 cells caused increased cell surface expression of MHC-I, which could be reversed by either uridine supplementation or by treatment with BMS-345541; neither uridine nor BMS-345541 alone affected cell surface MHC-I expression (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from HCT116 cells treated with BQ in combination with uridine or BMS-345541.

claim: Neither uridine nor BMS-345541 alone affected cell surface MHC-I expression in HCT116 cells.
source: Furthermore, BQ treatment (24 hr) of HCT116 cells caused increased cell surface expression of MHC-I, which could be reversed by either uridine supplementation or by treatment with BMS-345541; neither uridine nor BMS-345541 alone affected cell surface MHC-I expression (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from HCT116 cells treated with uridine or BMS-345541 alone.

claim: TPCA-1 is an established IKK2 inhibitor.
source: Given that TPCA-1 (an established IKK2 inhibitor; Podolin et al., 2005) did not block BQ-mediated APP induction (Figure 3A and C), we suspected that this effect of BMS-345541 was independent of IKK2.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study characterizing TPCA-1.

claim: The effect of BMS-345541 on blocking BQ-mediated APP induction is independent of IKK2.
source: Given that TPCA-1 (an established IKK2 inhibitor; Podolin et al., 2005) did not block BQ-mediated APP induction (Figure 3A and C), we suspected that this effect of BMS-345541 was independent of IKK2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that TPCA-1, another IKK2 inhibitor, did not block BQ-mediated APP induction.

claim: Increased APP mRNA expression was observed upon BQ, teriflunomide, or GSK983 treatment of either wild-type or IKK2-KO MiaPaCa2 cells.
source: Increased APP mRNA expression was observed upon BQ, teriflunomide, or GSK983 treatment (all DHODH inhibitors) of either wild-type or IKK2-KO MiaPaCa2 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from wild-type and IKK2-KO MiaPaCa2 cells treated with DHODH inhibitors.

claim: TNF-alpha stimulation induced APP and CCL5 expression in wild-type MiaPaCa2 cells, but not in IKK2-KO cells.
source: However, while TNF-alpha stimulation induced APP and CCL5 a canonical NF-κB target gene downstream of TNF-alpha (Yeo et al., 2020) expression in wild-type cells, this was not observed in IKK2-KO cells, as expected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, far right).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from wild-type and IKK2-KO MiaPaCa2 cells treated with TNF-alpha.

claim: CCL5 is a canonical NF-κB target gene downstream of TNF-alpha.
source: However, while TNF-alpha stimulation induced APP and CCL5 a canonical NF-κB target gene downstream of TNF-alpha (Yeo et al., 2020) expression in wild-type cells, this was not observed in IKK2-KO cells, as expected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, far right).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: BQ-mediated APP induction in IKK2-KO MiaPaCa2 cells was significantly reversed with concurrent BMS-345541 treatment.
source: Finally, BQ-mediated APP induction in IKK2-KO cells was significantly reversed with concurrent BMS-345541 treatment (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from IKK2-KO MiaPaCa2 cells treated with BQ in combination with BMS-345541.

claim: IKK2 is dispensable for BQ-mediated APP induction.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that IKK2 is dispensable for BQ-mediated APP induction and that the observed reversal effect of BMS-345541 is independent of IKK2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that BQ induces APP genes in IKK2-KO cells and that BMS-345541 blocks this induction in IKK2-KO cells.

claim: The observed reversal effect of BMS-345541 on BQ-mediated APP induction is independent of IKK2.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that IKK2 is dispensable for BQ-mediated APP induction and that the observed reversal effect of BMS-345541 is independent of IKK2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that BMS-345541 blocks BQ-mediated APP induction in IKK2-KO cells.

claim: BMS-345541 reproducibly bound more than 20 kinases in cell-free KINOMEscan assays, with dissociation constants (kd) ranging from 130 to 8100 nM.
source: BMS-345541 reproducibly bound more than 20 kinases, with dissociation constants (kd) ranging from 130 to 8100 nM (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by publicly available KINOMEscan data.

claim: One potential target of BMS-345541 that met the selection criteria was CDK9.
source: One potential target that met the selection criteria was CDK9, which together with cyclin T1 or T2 forms positive transcription elongation factor B (P-TEFb).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of KINOMEscan data and selection criteria for potential targets.

claim: CDK9 together with cyclin T1 or T2 forms positive transcription elongation factor B (P-TEFb).
source: One potential target that met the selection criteria was CDK9, which together with cyclin T1 or T2 forms positive transcription elongation factor B (P-TEFb).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the composition of P-TEFb.

claim: P-TEFb is required for the release of promoter-proximal paused RNA polymerase II (Pol II) into productive elongation.
source: P-TEFb is required for the release of promoter-proximal paused RNA polymerase II (Pol II) into productive elongation and therefore is essential for Pol II transcription from paused promoters (Price, 2000; Ni et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on P-TEFb function.

claim: P-TEFb is essential for Pol II transcription from paused promoters.
source: P-TEFb is required for the release of promoter-proximal paused RNA polymerase II (Pol II) into productive elongation and therefore is essential for Pol II transcription from paused promoters (Price, 2000; Ni et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on P-TEFb function.

claim: The potent P-TEFb inhibitor flavopiridol phenocopied BMS-345541 by blocking APP induction downstream of DHODH, IMPDH1/2, or CTP synthase inhibition.
source: The potent P-TEFb inhibitor flavopiridol (Chao et al., 2000) phenocopied BMS-345541 in our assays as it blocked APP induction downstream of DHODH, IMPDH1/2 (by mycophenolate), or CTP synthase (by 3-deazauridine McPartland et al., 1974) inhibition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HCT116 cells treated with nucleotide synthesis inhibitors in combination with flavopiridol.

claim: APP induction downstream of nucleotide starvation requires P-TEFb-mediated paused Pol II release.
source: This suggests that APP induction downstream of nucleotide starvation requires P-TEFb-mediated paused Pol II release.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that P-TEFb inhibitors block APP induction by nucleotide synthesis inhibitors.

claim: The BMS-345541 effect of reversing BQ-induced APP upregulation is due to P-TEFb inhibition.
source: It also suggests that the BMS-345541 effect of reversing BQ-induced APP upregulation is due to P-TEFb inhibition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that flavopiridol, a P-TEFb inhibitor, phenocopies BMS-345541.

claim: Two other CDK9 inhibitors (AT7519 and dinaciclib) phenocopied flavopiridol in blocking BQ-mediated APP induction in HEK-293T cells.
source: To further probe whether the observed effect of flavopiridol was due to CDK9 inhibition, we tested two other CDK9 inhibitors (AT7519 and dinaciclib). Both CDK9 inhibitors phenocopied flavopiridol in our assays (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HEK-293T cells treated with BQ in combination with various CDK9 inhibitors.

claim: A CDK9-targeted PROTAC (PROTAC2) blocked BQ-mediated APP induction in HEK-293T cells.
source: Furthermore, a previously characterized CDK9-targeted proteolysis targeting chimera (PROTAC), termed PROTAC2 (King et al., 2021), had the same effect (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HEK-293T cells treated with BQ in combination with PROTAC2.

claim: PROTAC2 consists of a CDK9-binding aminopyrazole warhead conjugated to pomalidomide, which recruits the E3 ubiquitin ligase Cereblon (CRBN).
source: PROTAC2 consists of a CDK9-binding aminopyrazole warhead conjugated to pomalidomide, which recruits the E3 ubiquitin ligase Cereblon (CRBN).
evidence: The claim is based on the published characterization of PROTAC2.

claim: Cereblon ubiquitinates CDK9, resulting in its proteasomal degradation when recruited by PROTAC2.
source: Cereblon in turn ubiquitinates CDK9, resulting in its proteasomal degradation.
evidence: The claim is based on the known mechanism of action of PROTACs and the published characterization of PROTAC2.

claim: Co-treatment of HEK-293T cells with PROTAC2 and pomalidomide prevents PROTAC2-mediated CDK9 degradation.
source: Co-treatment of HEK-293 cells with PROTAC2 and pomalidomide prevents PROTAC2-mediated CDK9 degradation, as free pomalidomide competes with PROTAC2 for Cereblon binding (King et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the published characterization of PROTAC2.

claim: Free pomalidomide competes with PROTAC2 for Cereblon binding.
source: Co-treatment of HEK-293 cells with PROTAC2 and pomalidomide prevents PROTAC2-mediated CDK9 degradation, as free pomalidomide competes with PROTAC2 for Cereblon binding (King et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the published characterization of PROTAC2.

claim: PROTAC2 (1 µM) blocked BQ-mediated APP induction in HEK-293T cells, and this effect was reversed by co-treatment with tenfold excess pomalidomide (10 µM).
source: We observed that PROTAC2 (1 µM) blocked BQ-mediated APP induction, and this effect was reversed by co-treatment with tenfold excess pomalidomide (10 µM); however, when we increased the concentration of PROTAC2 to 10 µM (so that PROTAC2 and pomalidomide concentrations were equal), pomalidomide no longer had this effect (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HEK-293T cells treated with BQ, PROTAC2, and pomalidomide at various concentrations.

claim: When PROTAC2 concentration was increased to 10 µM (equal to pomalidomide concentration), pomalidomide no longer reversed the effect of PROTAC2 on blocking BQ-mediated APP induction in HEK-293T cells.
source: We observed that PROTAC2 (1 µM) blocked BQ-mediated APP induction, and this effect was reversed by co-treatment with tenfold excess pomalidomide (10 µM); however, when we increased the concentration of PROTAC2 to 10 µM (so that PROTAC2 and pomalidomide concentrations were equal), pomalidomide no longer had this effect (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HEK-293T cells treated with BQ, PROTAC2, and pomalidomide at various concentrations.

claim: Immunoblot analysis showed that 10 µM pomalidomide prevents CDK9 degradation upon 1 µM but not 10 µM PROTAC2 treatment in HEK-293T cells.
source: Consistently, immunoblot analysis showed that 10 µM pomalidomide prevents CDK9 degradation upon 1 µM but not 10 µM PROTAC2 treatment (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data from HEK-293T cells treated with PROTAC2 and pomalidomide at various concentrations.

claim: All CDK9 inhibitors reversed BQ-mediated APP induction in HCT116 cells.
source: When we repeated the experiment shown in Figure 4B with HCT116 cells, we found that all CKD9 inhibitors reversed BQ-mediated APP induction, but PROTAC2 did not (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HCT116 cells treated with BQ in combination with various CDK9 inhibitors.

claim: PROTAC2 did not reverse BQ-mediated APP induction in HCT116 cells.
source: When we repeated the experiment shown in Figure 4B with HCT116 cells, we found that all CKD9 inhibitors reversed BQ-mediated APP induction, but PROTAC2 did not (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HCT116 cells treated with BQ in combination with PROTAC2.

claim: Immunoblot analysis showed that PROTAC2 did not cause CDK9 depletion in HCT116 cells.
source: Concordantly, immunoblot analysis showed that PROTAC2 did not cause CDK9 depletion in HCT116 cells treated in parallel (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data from HCT116 cells treated with PROTAC2.

claim: CDK9 degradation is necessary for the reversal effect of PROTAC2 on BQ-mediated APP induction.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that CDK9 degradation is necessary for the reversal effect of PROTAC2 and that CDK9 is required for BQ-mediated APP induction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that PROTAC2 only blocks BQ-mediated APP induction when it successfully degrades CDK9.

claim: CDK9 is required for BQ-mediated APP induction.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that CDK9 degradation is necessary for the reversal effect of PROTAC2 and that CDK9 is required for BQ-mediated APP induction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that multiple CDK9 inhibitors and CDK9 degradation block BQ-mediated APP induction.

claim: The dependence of BQ-mediated APP induction on CDK9 strongly suggests that nucleotide starvation enforces nascent transcription of APP genes, as opposed to increased mRNA stability.
source: The dependence of BQ-mediated APP induction on CDK9 strongly suggests that nucleotide starvation enforces nascent transcription of APP genes, as opposed to increased mRNA stability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the known role of CDK9 in transcription and the observation that CDK9 is required for BQ-mediated APP induction.

claim: The rapid buildup of APP transcripts following DHODH inhibitor treatment (within 4 hr) supports that nucleotide starvation enforces nascent transcription of APP genes.
source: This is further supported by the rapid buildup of APP transcripts following DHODH inhibitor treatment (within 4 hr, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data showing rapid increase in APP transcripts after DHODH inhibitor treatment.

claim: ChIP-seq analysis of global Pol II occupancy following 48 hr teriflunomide treatment in A375 cells shows increased Pol II occupancy across many APP genes.
source: Additionally, ChIP-seq analysis of global Pol II occupancy following 48 hr teriflunomide treatment in A375 cells (Tan et al., 2016) shows increased Pol II occupancy across many APP genes, and fold change in Pol II occupancy significantly correlated with fold change in mRNA expression under the same conditions (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of publicly available ChIP-seq data.

claim: Fold change in Pol II occupancy significantly correlated with fold change in mRNA expression following 48 hr teriflunomide treatment in A375 cells.
source: Additionally, ChIP-seq analysis of global Pol II occupancy following 48 hr teriflunomide treatment in A375 cells (Tan et al., 2016) shows increased Pol II occupancy across many APP genes, and fold change in Pol II occupancy significantly correlated with fold change in mRNA expression under the same conditions (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data from A375 cells treated with teriflunomide.

claim: Nucleotide starvation induces an antigen presentation gene expression program that is independent of canonical APP regulators but depends on CDK9/P-TEFb.
source: Overall, these results show that nucleotide starvation induces an antigen presentation gene expression program that is independent of canonical APP regulators but depends on CDK9/P-TEFb.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments showing that canonical APP pathway inhibitors do not block BQ-mediated APP induction, but CDK9 inhibitors do.

claim: Enforced MHC-I upregulation by various interventions can facilitate anticancer immunity and enhance the efficacy of ICB by antibodies directed at PD-(L)1 and/or CTLA-4.
source: Enforced MHC-I upregulation by various interventions can facilitate anticancer immunity and enhance the efficacy of ICB by antibodies directed at PD-(L)1 and/or CTLA-4 (Yamamoto et al., 2020; Goel et al., 2017; Kalbasi et al., 2020; Gu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: High MHC-I expression has been proposed as a predictor of ICB response.
source: Moreover, high MHC-I expression has been proposed as a predictor of ICB response (Rodig et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Grasso et al., 2020; Shklovskaya et al., 2020), and high expression of MHC-I and other APP genes, including NLRC5 and TAP1, correlates with better survival in patients with melanoma (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), for whom ICB is a first-line therapy.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: High expression of MHC-I and other APP genes, including NLRC5 and TAP1, correlates with better survival in patients with melanoma.
source: Moreover, high MHC-I expression has been proposed as a predictor of ICB response (Rodig et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Grasso et al., 2020; Shklovskaya et al., 2020), and high expression of MHC-I and other APP genes, including NLRC5 and TAP1, correlates with better survival in patients with melanoma (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), for whom ICB is a first-line therapy.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TCGA melanoma patient data.

claim: ICB is a first-line therapy for melanoma patients.
source: Moreover, high MHC-I expression has been proposed as a predictor of ICB response (Rodig et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Grasso et al., 2020; Shklovskaya et al., 2020), and high expression of MHC-I and other APP genes, including NLRC5 and TAP1, correlates with better survival in patients with melanoma (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), for whom ICB is a first-line therapy.
evidence: The claim is based on established clinical practice in melanoma treatment.

claim: The B16F10 melanoma immunocompetent mouse model is typically refractory to dual ICB (i.e., anti-PD-1 plus anti-CTLA-4).
source: Therefore, we asked if BQ could improve anticancer immunity in the B16F10 melanoma immunocompetent mouse model, which is typically refractory to dual ICB (i.e., anti-PD-1 plus anti-CTLA-4) (Twyman-Saint Victor et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: BQ (10 mg/kg daily IP injection) markedly suppressed tumor growth in the B16F10 melanoma model.
source: BQ (10 mg/kg daily IP injection) markedly suppressed tumor growth and led to reduced tumor burden (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor volume measurements from B16F10 tumor-bearing mice treated with BQ.

claim: BQ (10 mg/kg daily IP injection) led to reduced tumor burden in the B16F10 melanoma model.
source: BQ (10 mg/kg daily IP injection) markedly suppressed tumor growth and led to reduced tumor burden (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor weight and volume measurements at necropsy from B16F10 tumor-bearing mice treated with BQ.

claim: This is the first direct demonstration of BQ activity in the B16F10 melanoma model.
source: Historically, the lead tool compound that was ultimately modified to BQ (called NSC 339768) was prioritized in part based on its activity against B16 melanoma Dibner et al., 1985; however, to our knowledge, this is the first direct demonstration of BQ activity in this model system.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature and their own experimental results.

claim: BQ treatment caused marked buildup of metabolites upstream of DHODH in B16F10 tumors.
source: Consistent with our in vitro metabolomics data (Figure 1I and J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E), BQ treatment caused marked buildup of metabolites upstream of DHODH and depletion of downstream pyrimidine nucleotide species in B16F10 tumors (Figure 5C), confirming target engagement in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data from B16F10 tumors harvested from BQ-treated mice.

claim: BQ treatment caused depletion of downstream pyrimidine nucleotide species in B16F10 tumors.
source: Consistent with our in vitro metabolomics data (Figure 1I and J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E), BQ treatment caused marked buildup of metabolites upstream of DHODH and depletion of downstream pyrimidine nucleotide species in B16F10 tumors (Figure 5C), confirming target engagement in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data from B16F10 tumors harvested from BQ-treated mice.

claim: BQ treatment in B16F10 tumors confirms target engagement in vivo.
source: Consistent with our in vitro metabolomics data (Figure 1I and J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E), BQ treatment caused marked buildup of metabolites upstream of DHODH and depletion of downstream pyrimidine nucleotide species in B16F10 tumors (Figure 5C), confirming target engagement in vivo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from metabolomics data showing expected changes in pyrimidine pathway metabolites in BQ-treated tumors.

claim: Metabolomics analysis of BQ- and vehicle-treated B16F10 tumors separated in principal component analysis.
source: Metabolomics analysis of BQ- and vehicle-treated tumors separated in principal component analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and unsupervised hierarchical clustering (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), confirming the perturbation of tumor metabolism following DHODH inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by principal component analysis of metabolomics data from B16F10 tumors.

claim: Metabolomics analysis of BQ- and vehicle-treated B16F10 tumors separated in unsupervised hierarchical clustering.
source: Metabolomics analysis of BQ- and vehicle-treated tumors separated in principal component analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and unsupervised hierarchical clustering (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), confirming the perturbation of tumor metabolism following DHODH inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis of metabolomics data from B16F10 tumors.

claim: The separation of BQ- and vehicle-treated tumors in metabolomics analyses confirms the perturbation of tumor metabolism following DHODH inhibition.
source: Metabolomics analysis of BQ- and vehicle-treated tumors separated in principal component analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and unsupervised hierarchical clustering (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), confirming the perturbation of tumor metabolism following DHODH inhibition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the clear separation of treatment groups in metabolomics analyses.

claim: BQ-treated B16F10 tumors showed increased mRNA expression of MHC-I (H2-Db and H2-Kb) and Nlrc5.
source: BQ-treated B16F10 tumors showed increased mRNA expression of MHC-I (H2-Db and H2-Kb) and Nlrc5 (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from B16F10 tumors harvested from BQ-treated mice.

claim: BQ monotherapy conferred marked survival benefit in the B16F10 melanoma model.
source: Similar to its impressive activity in our first experiment (Figure 5A and B), BQ monotherapy conferred marked survival benefit.
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis of B16F10 tumor-bearing mice treated with BQ.

claim: BQ monotherapy survival benefit was significantly enhanced by subsequent dual ICB in the B16F10 melanoma model.
source: This was significantly enhanced by subsequent dual ICB, while dual ICB alone conferred only marginally prolonged survival, and concurrent BQ plus dual ICB did not significantly improve survival versus BQ monotherapy (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis comparing different treatment regimens in B16F10 tumor-bearing mice.

claim: Dual ICB alone conferred only marginally prolonged survival in the B16F10 melanoma model.
source: This was significantly enhanced by subsequent dual ICB, while dual ICB alone conferred only marginally prolonged survival, and concurrent BQ plus dual ICB did not significantly improve survival versus BQ monotherapy (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis of B16F10 tumor-bearing mice treated with dual ICB.

claim: Concurrent BQ plus dual ICB did not significantly improve survival versus BQ monotherapy in the B16F10 melanoma model.
source: This was significantly enhanced by subsequent dual ICB, while dual ICB alone conferred only marginally prolonged survival, and concurrent BQ plus dual ICB did not significantly improve survival versus BQ monotherapy (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis comparing BQ monotherapy to concurrent BQ plus dual ICB in B16F10 tumor-bearing mice.

claim: Sequential (rather than concurrent) administration of DHODH inhibitor and ICB may be superior.
source: This suggests that sequential (rather than concurrent) administration of DHODH inhibitor and ICB may be superior.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that BQ followed by ICB improved survival more than concurrent BQ plus ICB.

claim: BQ causes pyrimidine nucleotide depletion in the B16F10 melanoma model.
source: Taken together, these results show that BQ causes pyrimidine nucleotide depletion, MHC-I and APP gene transcriptional upregulation, and additive survival benefit with dual ICB in a highly aggressive and ICB-refractory mouse melanoma model.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data from B16F10 tumors.

claim: BQ causes MHC-I and APP gene transcriptional upregulation in the B16F10 melanoma model.
source: Taken together, these results show that BQ causes pyrimidine nucleotide depletion, MHC-I and APP gene transcriptional upregulation, and additive survival benefit with dual ICB in a highly aggressive and ICB-refractory mouse melanoma model.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from B16F10 tumors.

claim: BQ causes additive survival benefit with dual ICB in a highly aggressive and ICB-refractory mouse melanoma model.
source: Taken together, these results show that BQ causes pyrimidine nucleotide depletion, MHC-I and APP gene transcriptional upregulation, and additive survival benefit with dual ICB in a highly aggressive and ICB-refractory mouse melanoma model.
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data from B16F10 tumor-bearing mice treated with BQ followed by dual ICB.

claim: Pyrimidine nucleotide depletion by DHODH inhibition causes increased expression of APP genes and increased antigen presentation via MHC-I across a diverse panel of cancer cell lines.
source: Our results demonstrate that pyrimidine nucleotide depletion by DHODH inhibition causes increased expression of APP genes and increased antigen presentation via MHC-I across a diverse panel of cancer cell lines (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq, RT-qPCR, and flow cytometry data from multiple cancer cell lines treated with DHODH inhibitors.

claim: The effect of BQ and teriflunomide on APP gene expression is strictly dependent on pyrimidine nucleotide depletion.
source: This effect of BQ and teriflunomide is strictly dependent on pyrimidine nucleotide depletion, as it was abrogated by restoration of pyrimidine levels with exogenous uridine (Figure 2B–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that uridine supplementation blocks APP induction by DHODH inhibitors.

claim: Genetic deletion of DHODH recapitulated the effect of DHODH inhibitors on APP gene expression.
source: Furthermore, genetic deletion of DHODH recapitulated this effect, and treatment of DHODH knockout cells with BQ did not further increase MHC-I mRNA expression (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from DHODH knockout cells.

claim: BQ-mediated APP induction is independent of IFN-JAK-STAT, cGAS-STING-TBK1, and NF-κB pathways.
source: Our inhibitor reversal studies determined that BQ-mediated APP induction is independent of several canonical APP regulatory pathways, including IFN-JAK-STAT, cGAS-STING-TBK1, and NF-κB (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that inhibitors of these pathways do not block BQ-mediated APP induction.

claim: BQ-mediated APP induction relies on P-TEFb-mediated release of Pol II from promoter-proximal paused state to productive elongation.
source: We showed that this effect relies on P-TEFb-mediated release of Pol II from promoter-proximal paused state to productive elongation (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that P-TEFb inhibitors block BQ-mediated APP induction.

claim: Pharmacologic depletion of GTP (by IMPDH inhibition) or CTP (by CTPS inhibition) triggers APP upregulation in a P-TEFb-dependent manner.
source: These findings were extended to inhibition of IMPDH (which depletes cellular GTP) and CTPS (which depletes cellular CTP), as these effects were also reversible with P-TEFb inhibition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). This suggests that pharmacologic depletion of these nucleotide species also triggers APP upregulation in a P-TEFb-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that P-TEFb inhibitors block APP induction by IMPDH and CTPS inhibitors.

claim: Pretreatment with DHODH inhibitors can improve the efficacy of ICB in a highly aggressive and ICB-refractory mouse melanoma model.
source: We provide proof-of-concept evidence that pretreatment with DHODH inhibitors can improve the efficacy of ICB in a highly aggressive and ICB-refractory mouse melanoma model (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data from B16F10 tumor-bearing mice treated with BQ followed by dual ICB.

claim: BQ-mediated APP induction does not require interferon signaling.
source: Because BQ-mediated APP induction does not require interferon signaling, this strategy may have particular relevance for clinical scenarios in which tumor antigen presentation is dampened by the loss or silencing of cancer cell interferon signaling, which has been demonstrated to confer both intrinsic (Shin et al., 2017) and acquired (Zaretsky et al., 2016) ICB resistance in human melanoma patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that interferon pathway inhibitors do not block BQ-mediated APP induction.

claim: Loss or silencing of cancer cell interferon signaling has been demonstrated to confer both intrinsic and acquired ICB resistance in human melanoma patients.
source: Because BQ-mediated APP induction does not require interferon signaling, this strategy may have particular relevance for clinical scenarios in which tumor antigen presentation is dampened by the loss or silencing of cancer cell interferon signaling, which has been demonstrated to confer both intrinsic (Shin et al., 2017) and acquired (Zaretsky et al., 2016) ICB resistance in human melanoma patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Emerging evidence suggests that cancer cell MHC-I expression predicts favorable response to ICB.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that cancer cell MHC-I expression predicts favorable response to ICB, and several recent studies have shown that enforced cancer cell MHC-I expression enhances anticancer immunity and ICB efficacy in various mouse models.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' interpretation of recent literature in the field.

claim: Several recent studies have shown that enforced cancer cell MHC-I expression enhances anticancer immunity and ICB efficacy in various mouse models.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that cancer cell MHC-I expression predicts favorable response to ICB, and several recent studies have shown that enforced cancer cell MHC-I expression enhances anticancer immunity and ICB efficacy in various mouse models.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' interpretation of recent literature in the field.

claim: Functional genomic screens for regulators of cancer cell MHC-I expression have revealed novel molecular targets to induce cancer cell APP activity.
source: Accordingly, functional genomic screens for regulators of cancer cell MHC-I expression have recently been undertaken, and these efforts have revealed novel molecular targets to induce cancer cell APP activity (Gu et al., 2021; Dersh et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Agents shown to increase cancer cell antigen presentation include hydroxychloroquine (by autophagy inhibition).
source: Agents shown to increase cancer cell antigen presentation include hydroxychloroquine (by autophagy inhibition) (Yamamoto et al., 2020), poly(I:C) (by NF-κB activation downstream of dsRNA sensing) (Kalbasi et al., 2020), SMAC mimetics (by NF-κB activation) (Gu et al., 2021), CDK4/6 inhibitors (by activation of endogenous genomic retroviral elements) (Goel et al., 2017), and others.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Agents shown to increase cancer cell antigen presentation include poly(I:C) (by NF-κB activation downstream of dsRNA sensing).
source: Agents shown to increase cancer cell antigen presentation include hydroxychloroquine (by autophagy inhibition) (Yamamoto et al., 2020), poly(I:C) (by NF-κB activation downstream of dsRNA sensing) (Kalbasi et al., 2020), SMAC mimetics (by NF-κB activation) (Gu et al., 2021), CDK4/6 inhibitors (by activation of endogenous genomic retroviral elements) (Goel et al., 2017), and others.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Agents shown to increase cancer cell antigen presentation include SMAC mimetics (by NF-κB activation).
source: Agents shown to increase cancer cell antigen presentation include hydroxychloroquine (by autophagy inhibition) (Yamamoto et al., 2020), poly(I:C) (by NF-κB activation downstream of dsRNA sensing) (Kalbasi et al., 2020), SMAC mimetics (by NF-κB activation) (Gu et al., 2021), CDK4/6 inhibitors (by activation of endogenous genomic retroviral elements) (Goel et al., 2017), and others.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Agents shown to increase cancer cell antigen presentation include CDK4/6 inhibitors (by activation of endogenous genomic retroviral elements).
source: Agents shown to increase cancer cell antigen presentation include hydroxychloroquine (by autophagy inhibition) (Yamamoto et al., 2020), poly(I:C) (by NF-κB activation downstream of dsRNA sensing) (Kalbasi et al., 2020), SMAC mimetics (by NF-κB activation) (Gu et al., 2021), CDK4/6 inhibitors (by activation of endogenous genomic retroviral elements) (Goel et al., 2017), and others.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Many anticancer drugs likely perturb cancer cell antigen presentation and/or have other immunomodulatory properties in addition to their cell-intrinsic antiproliferative activity.
source: It is very likely that many other anticancer drugs perturb cancer cell antigen presentation and/or have other immunomodulatory properties in addition to their cell-intrinsic antiproliferative activity (Petroni et al., 2021), and this area requires further scrutiny.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' interpretation of the literature and is supported by a citation.

claim: DHODH inhibition is a powerful inducer of antigen presentation and MHC-I expression in diverse cancer cell lines and in HEK-293T cells.
source: In this study, we identified DHODH inhibition as a powerful inducer of antigen presentation and MHC-I expression in diverse cancer cell lines and in HEK-293T cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq, RT-qPCR, and flow cytometry data from multiple cell lines treated with DHODH inhibitors.

claim: Previous studies have linked pyrimidine depletion with upregulation of innate immunity and interferon-stimulated genes.
source: Previous studies have linked pyrimidine depletion with upregulation of innate immunity and interferon-stimulated genes (Lucas-Hourani et al., 2013; Sprenger et al., 2021) and this was confirmed by our transcriptomic profiling experiments (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies and is confirmed by the authors' own data.

claim: Lucas-Hourani et al. proposed that interferon-stimulated gene expression requires the DNA damage checkpoint kinase ATM.
source: Lucas-Hourani et al. proposed that interferon-stimulated gene expression requires the DNA damage checkpoint kinase ATM (Lucas-Hourani et al., 2013) while Sprenger et al. conclude that pyrimidine depletion causes accumulation of mitochondrial DNA in the cytosol, which is sensed by the cGAS-STING-TBK1 pathway to promote innate immunity (Sprenger et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Sprenger et al. conclude that pyrimidine depletion causes accumulation of mitochondrial DNA in the cytosol, which is sensed by the cGAS-STING-TBK1 pathway to promote innate immunity.
source: Lucas-Hourani et al. proposed that interferon-stimulated gene expression requires the DNA damage checkpoint kinase ATM (Lucas-Hourani et al., 2013) while Sprenger et al. conclude that pyrimidine depletion causes accumulation of mitochondrial DNA in the cytosol, which is sensed by the cGAS-STING-TBK1 pathway to promote innate immunity (Sprenger et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: In the authors' models, neither ATM/ATR nor TBK1 inhibition blocked BQ-mediated APP induction.
source: In our models, neither ATM/ATR nor TBK1 inhibition blocked BQ-mediated APP induction (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from cells treated with BQ in combination with ATM/ATR or TBK1 inhibitors.

claim: Pyrimidine nucleotide shortage may lead to APP induction by multiple redundant mechanisms, any of which may predominate based on the cellular context.
source: It is possible that pyrimidine nucleotide shortage leads to APP induction by multiple redundant mechanisms, any of which may predominate based on the cellular context.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning by the authors to explain discrepancies between their findings and previous studies.

claim: Cells may have evolved multiple means of sensing acute pyrimidine shortage as a way to detect viral infection or malignant transformation.
source: We speculate that cells may have evolved multiple means of sensing acute pyrimidine shortage as a way to detect viral infection or malignant transformation, as both viral replication and uncontrolled cell proliferation avidly consume nucleotides.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning by the authors.

claim: Both viral replication and uncontrolled cell proliferation avidly consume nucleotides.
source: We speculate that cells may have evolved multiple means of sensing acute pyrimidine shortage as a way to detect viral infection or malignant transformation, as both viral replication and uncontrolled cell proliferation avidly consume nucleotides.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about nucleotide consumption in viral replication and cell proliferation.

claim: IMPDH inhibition was shown to enhance ICB efficacy by favorably altering the MHC-I peptide repertoire and increasing immunoproteasome expression.
source: This is consistent with a recent study in which IMPDH inhibition was shown to enhance ICB efficacy by favorably altering the MHC-I peptide repertoire and increasing immunoproteasome expression (Keshet et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: In the Keshet et al. study, cancer cells were pretreated with IMPDH inhibitor before implantation into syngeneic hosts, and so possible countervailing immunosuppression by systemic IMPDH inhibitor treatment was not addressed.
source: However, in this study, the cancer cells were pretreated with IMPDH inhibitor before implantation into syngeneic hosts, and so possible countervailing immunosuppression by systemic IMPDH inhibitor treatment was not addressed (Keshet et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' interpretation of the experimental design in the cited study.

claim: The authors' in vivo results highlight the importance of timing/sequence when administering immunotherapy in combination with nucleotide synthesis inhibitors.
source: Our in vivo results (Figure 5E) highlight the importance of timing/sequence when administering immunotherapy in combination with nucleotide synthesis inhibitors and suggest that upfront BQ followed by ICB may be superior to concurrent administration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the survival data showing different outcomes with sequential versus concurrent administration.

claim: Upfront BQ followed by ICB may be superior to concurrent administration.
source: Our in vivo results (Figure 5E) highlight the importance of timing/sequence when administering immunotherapy in combination with nucleotide synthesis inhibitors and suggest that upfront BQ followed by ICB may be superior to concurrent administration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the survival data showing better outcomes with sequential administration.

claim: Thymidylate synthase inhibition was recently shown to induce MHC-I in a model of diffuse large B cell lymphoma.
source: Thymidylate synthase inhibition was recently shown to induce MHC-I in a model of diffuse large B cell lymphoma (Dersh et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The failure of thymidylate synthase inhibitors 5-fluorouracil and methotrexate to induce MHC-I in the authors' screen may be attributable to cell line differences (PDAC vs. DLBCL), dose/duration considerations, or the use of different thymidylate synthase inhibitors.
source: The failure of thymidylate synthase inhibitors 5-fluorouracil and methotrexate to induce MHC-I in our screen (Figure 2F) may be attributable to cell line differences (PDAC vs. DLBCL), dose/duration considerations, or the use of different thymidylate synthase inhibitors than in their study (which used pemetrexed and raltitrexed).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning by the authors to explain discrepancies between their findings and a published study.

claim: The abundance of multiple nucleotide species can exert context-dependent influence on MHC and APP gene expression.
source: Thus, it appears that the abundance of multiple nucleotide species can exert context-dependent influence on MHC and APP gene expression, and key details of this relationship remain to be elucidated.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that different nucleotide synthesis inhibitors can induce APP genes under different conditions.

claim: Key details of the relationship between nucleotide abundance and MHC/APP gene expression remain to be elucidated.
source: Thus, it appears that the abundance of multiple nucleotide species can exert context-dependent influence on MHC and APP gene expression, and key details of this relationship remain to be elucidated.
evidence: The claim acknowledges gaps in current understanding based on the authors' findings.

claim: The study establishes P-TEFb and Pol II elongation control as a mechanistic link between nucleotide depletion and APP induction.
source: Overall, our study establishes P-TEFb and Pol II elongation control as a mechanistic link between nucleotide depletion and APP induction.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments showing that P-TEFb inhibitors block APP induction by nucleotide synthesis inhibitors.

claim: The study provides proof-of-concept evidence for combinatorial benefit of DHODH inhibition and ICB in an aggressive and poorly immunogenic mouse model of melanoma.
source: We provide proof-of-concept evidence for combinatorial benefit of DHODH inhibition and ICB in an aggressive and poorly immunogenic mouse model of melanoma.
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data from B16F10 tumor-bearing mice treated with BQ followed by dual ICB.

claim: A deeper understanding of metabolic control of antigen presentation will enable rational therapy development for cancer and viral infection.
